To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) panels of human cell-lines derived from non-semanomatous germ cell tumors and transitional cell carcinomata of the bladder may provide useful information in the screening of new anticancer drugs; 2) the compounds that were screened were either inactive in the P388 assay in vivo or had been retested against the human tumour cell colony-forming assay and in some cases against human tumours xenografts; 3) the most selective compound was chloroquinoxiline
panels of human bladder cancer and testicular germ cell tumour cell lines are useful for screening novel anticancer agents.

(i) the clonogenic assay is a useful method for screening new compounds for anticancer activity; (ii) the use of panels of cell lines from nonseminomatous germ-cell tumours and bladder carcinomas is a useful addition to conventional screening methods; and (iii) a number of new compounds with selective anticancer activity are worthy of further study.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and applying novel methods to the discovery of anticancer agents.
the discovery of novel anticancer drugs and the elucidation of their mechanism of action.
the identification of novel compounds with anticancer activity, and the elucidation of the mechanisms of action and resistance of these agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the panels were useful in the selection of compounds with activity against bladder tumour, but were not helpful in the selection of agents with activity against testis tumour.
the HTCA is an effective and efficient method for screening anticancer compounds.
the HT-29 cell line is not suitable for the screening of anticancer agents.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the HTCA is a useful screening tool in the early stages of drug discovery and the HTCA is useful for the identification of new anticancer drugs with a high degree of specificity for certain tumour types.
the use of panels of tumour cell lines in screening programmes can provide useful information about differential toxicity.
the HTCA is a valuable tool to screen new agents for activity against human cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of panels of cell lines derived from human tumours may be a useful adjunct to the current disease-oriented screening programme for novel anticancer agents.
the testis tumour panel is a useful tool for the screening of anticancer agents.
there is an urgent need to develop new drugs for the treatment of advanced bladder cancer and that the use of cell line-based screening approaches may be useful in this regard.
